projects.title: Starship Booster Cryo Proof Tooling
projects.summary: I redesigned Super Heavy’s cryo-proof tooling to reduce leak paths and make installation repeatable: welded drain elbows, a GOX seal interface, and standard attachment bolts, carried from load calculations into vehicle integration.

points.text: The cryo-proof assembly had leak-prone interfaces, difficult work access, and opportunities for incorrect assembly. I redesigned the tooling sealing the booster’s 33 feedlines.

Reduce leak-prone interfaces in the test assembly to improve cryo-proof data collection. Redesign components to shorten integration time and move assembly work upstream, off the critical path of on-vehicle production.

I replaced a leak-prone bolted joint stackup with a welded 90° elbow connecting the blankoff to the cryogenic drain tube. The elbow welded directly to the blankoff, leaving one B-nut joint at the flared tube’s AN connection with a copper seal. I chose 304 stainless steel to match the blankoff’s weld material. I used the maximum elbow outlet moment and loads from the cryo-proof feedline blow-off cases to size the elbow’s vehicle-side weld to the blankoff using Blodgett’s method. A radial key clocked the outlet; a diameter step located weld height. I toleranced the fit to keep the TIG root gap within 0.5 mm. I ran Ansys simulations on the revised blankoff geometries, including the new clocking cutouts. I applied pressure to their internal faces based on the maximum feedline blow-off load cases in the cryo-proof test. I designed a Monel bung welded to a stainless blankoff to improve sealing performance at another faulty interface. I controlled the interface geometry to minimize gaseous-oxygen (GOX) impingement risk and sized the dissimilar-metal weld using Blodgett’s method. The bung protruded through the blankoff and sat against a counterbore in the blankoff to form the inner lip of an upper seal gland. I used the Parker O-Ring Handbook to size the gland for the required O-ring compression. I evaluated replacing the existing A280 mil-spec bolts with Grade 5 hardware stocked in the factory. I based the sizing on maximum feedline blow-off loads during cryo-proof testing. From the blow-off force, I calculated the required bolt preload and tightening torque using T = KDF. I checked joint gapping and bolt fatigue under repeated loading. All checks passed, allowing us to replace the specialized bolts with standard Grade 5 hardware.
I released the revised parts, evaluated manufacturing deviations against critical sealing requirements, and oversaw welded-subassembly fabrication and vehicle integration.

I rerouted drain tubes for work access and mistake-proofed an asymmetric subassembly. I maintained the 13,000-component CAD assembly across three vehicle release states and designed lineside storage to support two vehicles using the tools simultaneously.

projects.title: Brake Rotors & Mounts
projects.summary: I designed the rotor and mount for reliable braking within the drivetrain package, combining material tradeoffs, thermal analysis, structural FEA, and temperature testing.

points.text: I needed a reliable brake rotor and mount that fit the rear drivetrain package while limiting heat transfer into the mount.
Package the mount at the differential bolts, accommodate braking loads, and size the rotor for a 500°C temperature requirement with a safety margin.

I compared cast iron and 4140 steel and selected steel for its endurance-limit advantage. Titanium buttons limited heat transfer into the 7075 aluminum mount, which I packaged at the differential bolts.

For the 500°C requirement, I first sized thickness assuming maximum braking energy became heat with no heat escaping. I refined that conservative estimate with transient conduction, forced convection, and radiation analysis. I added curved face slots for debris removal, de-gassing, and water clearance, accepting additional pad wear. In Ansys, I supported the pad contact regions and applied braking moment through the mount connections to check stress.

The face slots improved debris, gas, and water clearance at the cost of additional pad wear. Sponsorship availability drove the Brembo P2.34 caliper choice; the supporting matrix records the technical tradeoffs.

projects.headline: Brake Rotors & Mounts
projects.challenge: Coordinate the rotor packaging with the powertrain team and design for long-term reliability, with a 500°C temperature requirement and a safety margin.
projects.decision: Compare cast iron with 4140 steel, use titanium buttons to limit heat flow into an aluminum mount, and refine rotor thickness through transient thermal analysis.
projects.proof: Checked the rotor in Ansys with supports at the pad contact regions and braking moment applied through the mount bolt locations. Used temperature crayons to assess operating temperatures and outsourced manufacturing to a three-axis CNC supplier.
projects.takeaway: Long-term reliability guided the material choices, thermal sizing, and structural checks.

caliperSelection.rationale: Sponsorship availability was the deciding factor. The Brembo had the largest listed pad area, tied the ISR for the largest listed piston area, and weighed less than the ISR. The AP Racing option was lighter and the Wilwood was less expensive; the comparison did not identify a clear winner across all criteria.

projects.title: V3 Starfactory Weld Cell & Integration Tooling
projects.summary: I owned the CONOPS, layout, and tooling design for a V3 Starfactory cell building a ring manifold for oxygen, methane, environmental-control gases, and helium. I carried the work from fixture prototypes through machined tooling, lift planning, and vehicle integration.

points.text: As SpaceX redesigned the factory line for Starship V3, I owned the CONOPS, layout, tooling design, and integration of a new build cell for a welded ring manifold of tubes extending 360° around the vehicle’s inner circumference.

Design the cell’s CONOPS for a target production rate of one completed assembly every 30 hours at full rate. Build tooling to clock critical tube endpoints within a 5° angular profile, with ±1 mm of translational freedom along the barrel’s inner circumference. Design a lift tool with a 1,100 lb working load limit and proof-test it at 2× WLL.

I used PLA for printed fixture prototypes, then primarily aluminum for the machined fixtures to keep them light under modest loads. The lift tool used carbon steel with corrosion-resistant paint to prevent corrosion from spreading to flight hardware.

I designed fixtures that located from the Siegmund weld table’s hole pattern, leaving clearance around weld joints for the Orbitalum tube welders. The tooling controlled the manifold’s radius to match the vehicle’s inner diameter and located critical tube endpoints within a 5° clocking profile and ±1 mm along the barrel’s inner circumference. I used 3-2-1 locating principles, GD&T, and selected dowel-pin fits to size and tolerance the endpoint tools. I sized the tools’ seal glands using the Parker O-Ring Handbook. I quickly 3D-printed PLA fixture components for the first article build, revised the designs from those fit-up lessons, and had predominantly aluminum tools machined for subsequent builds. I oversaw the cell’s setup and integration. I worked with the assembly’s Responsible Engineer to establish rigging points on its brackets, then designed a three-point lift and rigging plan to fly the welded manifold into the vehicle. I used bending and deflection calculations to size the 1,100 lb WLL tool. I calculated bracket centers of gravity and placed welded lifting lugs directly above them to prevent tilt. I sized the lug welds so two lugs could carry the entire assembly. I proof-tested the tool at 2,200 lb, twice its working load limit, and wrote the integration plan for welding the subassembly on the vehicle. I designed a stand to improve work access during aft flap torque-frame integration. I based its load cases on the maximum forces technicians could apply during assembly. I solved for two-plane bending and maximum torsion, then used those loads to size the integration stand and its welds. I took precise measurements of existing assemblies and created as-built CAD models of the off-nominal conditions. I used those models to design five flight-part retrofits for manufacture and installation on the existing assemblies.
I also designed miscellaneous integration aids, including 3D-printed and Protolabs parts, to support the cell’s production process.

projects.challenge: Control manifold flange fit-up and improve access and handling during Starship assembly.
projects.decision: Use self-clocking weld fixtures, load-sized handling tools, and measured as-built CAD for flight-part retrofits.

projects.title: Rear Wheel Hub & Bearing Assembly
projects.summary: I designed a rear hub and bearing assembly that brought the drivetrain, wheel, and electronics interfaces together in a lightweight, manufacturable package.

points.text: I needed a lightweight rear hub that joined the drivetrain, wheel, bearing, and electronics interfaces while remaining practical to machine.
Accommodate the tripod bearing and Hall sensors, carry wheel and drivetrain loads, and package the bearing within an 80–85 mm bore and 110–120 mm outer-diameter envelope.
I compared titanium, 6061, and 7075 aluminum and selected 7075-T6. Its higher yield strength than 6061 supported the hub’s structural requirements.

I screened bearings in SKF SimPro Quick for load capacity, fatigue life, and power loss. Our initial choice, the SKF 71817 ACDGB/VQ253 angular-contact bearing, exceeded our budget, so we selected the SKF 61916-2RZ deep-groove ball bearing as the most practical option. Its dimensions set the hub’s packaging and thickness requirements. I built the initial hub geometry around the given packaging constraints and interface requirements from the drivetrain, wheel, bearing, and electronics systems. I sized hub-nut engagement using bolt tensile and nut thread-shear areas. In Ansys, I applied wheel loads from the team’s truss solver to the wheel flange, modeled the tensile load from the center-lock nut, and included bearing forces and drivetrain torque at the tripod interface. I used the FEA results to identify where I could remove material, then iterated on the pockets and rechecked the revised hub in Ansys.
Rotational features were turned first; CNC milling then produced the tripod cutout, pin and button holes, and flange pockets.
Bearing selection and machining access constrained where I could remove material.

projects.headline: Rear Wheel Hub & Bearing Assembly
projects.challenge: Define a rear hub assembly around the drivetrain’s tripod bearing and the electronics team’s Hall effect sensors, while meeting structural and manufacturing requirements.
projects.decision: Use the system interfaces and bearing selection to establish the hub geometry and thickness, compare titanium with 6061 and 7075 aluminum, then size the threaded hub nut connection and optimize pocketing with FEA.
projects.proof: Checked cornering and braking loads, bearing performance in SKF SimPro Quick, and hub behavior in Ansys. Manufacturing included lathe operations on several features and tooling the part for a three-axis CNC mill.
projects.takeaway: The drivetrain and electronics interfaces set the requirements. Bearing selection, structural analysis, and machining constraints then shaped the hub.

bearingSelection.method: Build the assembly in SKF SimPro Quick and sweep the candidate bearings. Work with Powertrain to set the allowable inner diameter.
bearingSelection.validation: Selected the SKF 61916-2RZ deep-groove ball bearing after reviewing fatigue life, load capacity, and power loss across wheel speeds.

projects.title: Carbon Pushrod & Swept Control Arms
projects.summary: I developed and fabricated a lighter suspension assembly, pairing carbon-fiber pushrods with steel control arms and checking both the bonded joints and on-car clearance.

points.text: I redesigned and fabricated the control arms and pushrods to reduce suspension mass while preserving their interfaces and on-car clearance.
Connect the upright, chassis tabs, and pushrods; carry tension and compression loads; control the bonded end-plug fit; and maintain clearance through maximum steer.

I retained steel control arms because the team had greater confidence in that manufacturing process. Carbon-fiber pushrods reduced mass, with turned aluminum end plugs providing the bonded connections.
I replaced a heavy mounting plate with gussets at the control-arm apex. I tested the carbon-fiber pushrods in tension and compression on an Instron.

I cut the carbon tubes and turned their end plugs, controlling bonding-surface diameter within 0.0005 in. For the control arms, I cut steel tubing, turned and milled plugs, bored and reamed bearing seats, and welded and tapped rod-end interfaces.

During freshman-year integration, a missed tolerance stackup caused the apex to interfere at maximum steer. We checked the required material removal in Ansys and ground the existing apex to recover clearance.

gallery.cap: Upper apex von Mises: 38.6 ksi max

projects.headline: Pushrods & Control Arms
projects.unit: less suspension mass than the prior design
projects.challenge: At integration, the control-arm apex interfered before the car reached maximum steer. A tolerance stackup we had missed in the design caused the clearance problem.
projects.decision: Model the exact material removal needed at the apex, check the revised geometry in Ansys, then use an angle grinder to remove that material from the existing part.
projects.proof: The revised apex made maximum steer possible. The original suspension redesign saved 4.6 lb through the apex-mounted gussets and carbon-fiber pushrods.
projects.takeaway: That experience taught me how much engineering is working through the problem in front of you, one constraint at a time.

outline.title: Problem statement
outline.text: I redesigned and fabricated the control arms and pushrods to reduce suspension mass while preserving their interfaces and on-car clearance.

outline.title: Design requirements
outline.text: Connect the upright, chassis tabs, and pushrods; carry tension and compression loads; control the bonded end-plug fit; and maintain clearance through maximum steer.

outline.title: Material selection
outline.text: I retained steel control arms because the team had greater confidence in that manufacturing process. Carbon-fiber pushrods reduced mass, with turned aluminum end plugs providing the bonded connections.

projects.title: Discrete Ride Height Adjustment
projects.summary: I designed a shim-based attachment to make ride-height changes more repeatable, replacing a process that relied on turning a threaded rod-end.

points.text: Ride-height adjustment relied on turning a threaded rod-end. I designed a shim-based attachment for more repeatable setup changes.
Change pushrod length in discrete increments, retain the inboard suspension interface, and keep the shim stack in compression under pushrod loading.
I used 7075 aluminum for the attachment and minimized shim mass through lightweight geometry.
Adding or removing shims changes pushrod length; retightening the fasteners secures the setting. I kept the shim pockets concentric with the retaining bolts.
The shims were laser-cut and the attachment pieces machined. Another team member handled the upper component’s CNC machining.
The mechanism added 0.7 lb across the car in exchange for more repeatable ride-height adjustment.

projects.headline: Discrete Ride-Height Adjustment
projects.unit: added to the entire car for adjustability
projects.challenge: Make trackside ride-height changes more repeatable and easier to perform.
projects.decision: Use a 7075 aluminum attachment with removable shims for repeatable ride-height adjustment.
projects.proof: SolidWorks FEA checked the attachment under pushrod loading. The mechanism added 0.7 lb across the car.
projects.takeaway: A small weight penalty bought a more repeatable adjustment for the team at the track.

code.name: PolicyMarket

code.shotCap: Full bracket from a 10,000-run simulation, with per-matchup advance probabilities.
